article.overview: A radio beacon is a transmitter that broadcasts a known radio signal so that a receiver can work out its position, velocity or time from the received signal. On the Moon, surface and near-surface beacons are being studied as local navigation references, because a GPS-like signal source around the Moon is still being built. In the sources reviewed for this article, the only flown example identified is NASA's Lunar Node-1 (LN-1), which reached the lunar surface on Intuitive Machines' IM-1 mission on 22 February 2024 and conducted limited surface operations [2][3]. A second example, the ESA NAVISP Moon Station demonstrator, was tested on the ground and has not been reported as flown [5][6].
article.description: A radio beacon for navigation generates a signal with a known structure and timing. A user receiver measures either the signal's travel time, from which a range is derived when the transmit time is referenced to a common clock, or the frequency shift caused by motion, known as Doppler. Combining measurements from several sources allows a position fix. The beacon may be a fixed surface transmitter or a payload on a lander or orbiter. The term 'radio beacon' is used here for the payload class covered by catalogue entry 174. The two examples in this article are both described in the sources as navigation-oriented rather than general-purpose communication transmitters.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose is to provide navigation and timing references for surface and near-surface users such as landers, rovers and astronauts, and to test how such references can be combined with orbital signals. NASA states that LN-1 was meant to demonstrate navigation technologies, including the Multi-spacecraft Autonomous Positioning System (MAPS) algorithms, for lunar surface and orbital operations [2]. The LN-1 research team describes surface pseudolites (ground-based navigation transmitters) as a way to cover mid-latitude areas where orbital relays are limited [3]. Press coverage describes the Moon Station as a fixed surface beacon that generates ranging signals for nearby users and broadcasts differential corrections [5]. ESA NAVISP lists the Moon Station as project EL1-062, the Lunar Surface PNT Beacon Demonstrator [6].
article.operating_principle: Most lunar navigation beacons in the sources use ranging and Doppler measurements. In one-way pseudonoise (PN) ranging, the beacon transmits a code with a known structure, and the receiver estimates the signal's travel time by comparing the received code with its own reference copy. This requires the beacon's clock to be accurately related to a reference time. The LN-1 payload carried a Space Chip Scale Atomic Clock to discipline its S-band transmitter, and its tests compared time-based transfer and one-way PN ranging against one-way and two-way Doppler tracking [3]. The LunaNet Interoperability Specification defines the GNSS-like Augmented Forward Signal (AFS). The AFS uses a Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) signal at a single centre frequency in the 2483.5 to 2500 MHz band (S-band). Users can compute position, velocity and time when four or more signals are observed at once [1]. The same specification defines interfaces between lunar surface nodes and user surface nodes, but the sources reviewed do not describe a separate signal standard for surface beacons [1]. The Moon Station concept adds differential corrections. A surface station estimates the errors affecting nearby users and broadcasts them so that those users can improve their own solutions [5].
article.scientific_importance: A navigation beacon on the surface can serve as a reference that is not limited to orbital geometry. The LN-1 paper states that surface pseudolites could fit a broader lunar navigation architecture, including mid-latitude coverage where orbital relays are limited [3]. The importance of LN-1 is therefore mainly demonstrational: it provides flight data on whether a surface transmitter can be tracked and used for ranging from Earth's Deep Space Network. However, the sources reviewed do not publish final ranging accuracy, clock performance or MAPS solution results for the flight, so the scientific and engineering value of the measurements cannot yet be quantified from this research [3]. The Moon Station's ground-tested results point to a possible role for surface corrections, but the press account reports the benefit only as a qualitative reduction in user range errors, without a published figure [5].

physical_specifications.note: There is no single standard mass or size for a lunar radio beacon. The values below relate to two specific examples: one flown demonstrator and one ground-tested European concept. Values not stated in the sources reviewed are marked as not stated or null.

examples.name: Lunar Node-1 (LN-1)
examples.type: Flown lunar surface navigation beacon demonstrator, with limited surface operations
examples.mission_and_lander: Intuitive Machines IM-1 mission, lander Odysseus (NOVA-C class), landed 22 February 2024
examples.mass_note: Approximately 2.8 kg, according to NASA's pre-flight article.
examples.dimensions_note: Not used. The same NASA article gives a volume of approximately 175 x 220 x 300 cm, which is not consistent with a 2.8 kg beacon and has not been verified.
examples.power_note: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.radio: S-band navigation beacon. The specific frequency and bandwidth are not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.timing: Transmitter disciplined by a Space Chip Scale Atomic Clock.
examples.signals: One-way PN ranging, time-based transfer and one-way transmissions received by Deep Space Network ground stations.
examples.pre_flight_qualification: Vibration, electromagnetic interference and thermal-vacuum testing at Marshall in 2020 and 2021, and radio-frequency compatibility testing with the Deep Space Network at DTF-21 in early 2021.
examples.surface_operations: Limited. The payload transmitted to the Deep Space Network during transit and on two surface passes.
examples.survival: Not designed to survive the lunar night.

examples.name: ESA NAVISP Moon Station (Lunar Surface PNT Beacon Demonstrator)
examples.type: Ground-tested proposed surface positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) beacon and reference station. Not reported as flown.
examples.developers: Qascom as prime contractor, with OHB Italia as subcontractor, as reported in the sources reviewed.
examples.mass_note: Roughly 180 kg, as reported in press coverage.
examples.power_note: Around 440 W peak, as reported in press coverage.
examples.intended_site: Design assumption of a location near the lunar South Pole.
examples.functions: A fixed beacon that transmits ranging signals, computes and broadcasts differential corrections, and collects satellite observations from the surface.
examples.hardware: A navigation receiver for the lunar satellite navigation service, a configurable navigation beacon transmitter and communication modules for lunar users, orbiting satellites and Earth.
examples.test_status: An end-to-end testbed using an elegant breadboard demonstrator, tested on the ground.
examples.thermal_design: Analyses cover survival, active and operative modes through the lunar day-night cycle, with temperatures reported to fall below minus 150 degrees Celsius.
examples.performance_claims: Simulations combining a digital elevation model with extended Kalman filter processing are reported to reach meter-level positioning accuracy. The press account does not give numerical error-reduction values for the hardware test.
examples.technology_readiness_note: Not stated in the sources reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No verified dimensions are given for LN-1; the NASA volume figure is treated as unreliable. The Moon Station dimensions are not stated in the sources reviewed. A surface beacon's dimensions would be set by its antenna, clock, power and thermal design, and by the mounting needed to keep its antenna in view of users.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The LN-1 mass of approximately 2.8 kg and the Moon Station mass of roughly 180 kg illustrate a very wide range between a small demonstrator and a fixed station with power and thermal infrastructure. The mass drives lander capacity, mounting and deployment design, so the two values should not be treated as comparable performance measures.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LN-1 power is not stated in the sources reviewed. The Moon Station is reported at around 440 W peak power [5]. Long-term operation of a surface beacon through the lunar night would require power generation and storage; LN-1's designers noted this without giving figures [2].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A surface beacon must operate through the lunar day-night cycle, with large temperature swings. The Moon Station analysis covers thermal modes across this cycle, with temperatures reported below minus 150 degrees Celsius [5]. LN-1 was not designed to survive the lunar night, and its designers noted that longer operation would need adequate power generation and storage, without giving figures [2]. The sources reviewed do not provide beacon-specific test data for dust, radiation or micrometeoroid exposure.
article.limitations: A single beacon gives one range or Doppler measurement from one location and cannot by itself provide a position fix. A user needs several signals, or other information such as a terrain model. The LN-1 paper lists the near/far problem, in which a strong nearby signal can drown out weaker distant ones, among the challenges for surface pseudolites [3]. Coverage from a surface beacon is local, and a surface beacon would need power, thermal survival and calibration. The sources reviewed do not allow a conclusion about how much a surface beacon improves on other methods that do not use one.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The LN-1 payload was delivered to the surface as a payload on Intuitive Machines' NOVA-C lander, which touched down on 22 February 2024 [2][3]. For the Moon Station, the sources reviewed describe a fixed surface station but not its delivery or deployment method.
transportation_process: Integrate the beacon payload on the lander on Earth.
Launch the lander and transfer it towards the Moon.
Transmit to Deep Space Network ground stations during transit (LN-1 transmitted almost daily during transit).
Land on the surface, then conduct limited surface transmissions (LN-1).
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: LN-1 was carried as a payload on the NOVA-C lander and operated from the lander after landing; no separate deployment mechanism is described in the sources reviewed. The Moon Station deployment method is not described in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: LN-1 on Intuitive Machines' IM-1 mission (landed 22 February 2024) is the flown example identified in this research [2][3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with any named lander has not been verified from interface evidence beyond the LN-1 flight on NOVA-C [2][3]. The Moon Station's compatibility with a lander has not been assessed in the sources reviewed.

article.historical_significance: LN-1 was funded as a demonstration under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative and flown on a commercial lander [2]. NASA's account reports that the beacon was tested during the mission, with limited surface operations [2][3]. The flight is significant as a test of a surface navigation beacon carried by a commercial lunar lander, with limited results published so far [2][3].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Several numbers in this article come from a single source each. The LN-1 mass comes from a NASA article written before the flight, which is written in the future tense and does not report flight results [2]. The flight paper gives no numerical ranging accuracy, clock stability or MAPS solution values in the portion reviewed, so the full paper should be checked before any quantitative claim is made [3]. The LN-1 frequency and power are not stated. The Moon Station mass and power come from press coverage rather than an ESA technical document, and no technology readiness level is given [5][6]. The sources reviewed contain no compatibility assessment with a named lander beyond the LN-1 flight on NOVA-C [2][3]. The LunaNet document cited is the version 5 baseline dated 29 January 2025, and later revisions may differ [1].

Image URLs were taken from NASA article HTML via a fetch summary and were not downloaded, so direct_image_assets_verified_from_official_pages is false. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: The LN-1 volume figure on the NASA pre-flight page (approximately 175 x 220 x 300 cm) is inconsistent with the stated 2.8 kg mass and was not used; dimensions are set to null.
LN-1 frequency, power, and quantitative ranging, clock and MAPS results are not stated in the sources reviewed. The full NTRS 20240011676 paper should be read before any quantitative claim is added.
The NASA LN-1 article is a pre-flight article written in the future tense. Flight facts (landing 22 February 2024, limited surface operations) are taken from the NTRS flight paper.

The Moon Station mass (roughly 180 kg) and peak power (around 440 W) come from press coverage (Inside GNSS, February 2026), not from an ESA technical document. Its technology readiness level is not stated.
The Moon Station benefit of differential corrections is reported qualitatively; no numerical error-reduction figure is given.
The ESA NAVISP project listing (reference 6) was identified from search results and not opened in full; it is cited only for project identity.
The 2483.5 to 2500 MHz band is the LunaNet AFS band. The sources reviewed do not state the frequencies used by LN-1 or the Moon Station.

Image URLs were taken from NASA article HTML via a fetch summary and were not downloaded or checked byte-for-byte. Neither image shows the LN-1 beacon hardware itself. No verified image of the Moon Station was found.
